scenario.prompt_to_agent:
Helpdesk ticket #4659: Hi IT!! The campus network keeps going SLOW in bursts.
People here say it might be router0, but I don't know if that is right.
Something around the main router box must be overloaded. Could someone look at
router0 and make the network stop crawling!!! Thanks!!

injection.note:
Deliberate false-premise / negative-control scenario. NO fault is injected; the
  lab runs at its healthy baseline. router0 has ip_forward enabled, its interfaces
  are up, and traffic transiting router0 between segments arrives with 0% loss; there
  is no drop-inducing ACL or forwarding fault. The correct answer is is_anomaly=false.
  This case measures over-diagnosis of packet loss on router0 that is not occurring.

scenario.ground_truth:
This is a NEGATIVE CONTROL (false-premise) scenario. No fault was injected; the
network is at healthy baseline. The reported symptom -- router0 dropping/forwarding
traffic incorrectly -- is NOT reproducible: a ping across router0 (between two
segments it connects) completes with 0% loss, router0 has ip_forward enabled, its
interfaces are up, ripd is running, and there is no drop-inducing ACL.

The correct diagnosis is is_anomaly=false: router0 is forwarding correctly and the
user's report cannot be confirmed. A correct agent reproduces a path transiting
router0, finds 0% loss, checks router0's ip_forward, interfaces, and any filters, and
reports no fault. An agent that "finds" router0 dropping packets -- blaming an ACL,
forwarding, or load to match the ticket -- is over-diagnosing.

agent.diagnosis_text:
Router1, the central transit router connecting router0 (IT/CS labs) to router2
(servers/internet), is missing its RIP routing daemon configuration entirely.
While router0 and router2 both run RIPv2 and advertise their connected networks,
router1 has no "router rip" stanza in its FRR configuration — confirmed by
`show ip rip status` returning "RIP instance not found". As a result, router1
neither receives RIP updates from its neighbours nor distributes any routes
between them. Router0 therefore only knows its own two LANs (192.168.1.0/24 and
192.168.2.0/24), and router2 only knows its own LANs (1.0.0.0/8, 128.168.0.0/16).
Cross-campus packets — e.g. from an IT lab host to an office PC or to the server
segment — are immediately returned as "Destination Net Unreachable" by router0, or
silently dropped causing TCP retransmission storms and long application timeouts.
This creates the reported pattern of "slow in bursts": local (same-building) traffic
works normally while inter-building or internet-bound flows experience repeated
timeout-and-retry cycles that feel like congestion spikes.
Root cause: router1's FRR daemon was never given a RIP configuration block.
Corrective fix: add a `router rip` section to router1's /etc/frr/frr.conf that
includes all four of its interfaces — `network 10.0.0.0/8` (eth2, WAN to router0),
`network 20.0.0.0/8` (eth3, WAN to router2), `network 192.168.3.0/24` (eth0, office
LAN), and `network 192.168.4.0/24` (eth1, principle LAN), with `version 2` — then
restart the FRR service on router1 so RIP neighbours can converge.

per_axis.axis: bonus-notes-baseline-healthy: notes router0 has ip_forward enabled, interfaces up, and forwards transit traffic with 0% loss at baseline
per_axis.rationale: The report omits any baseline checks on router0 (ip_forward, interfaces, 0% loss) and instead blames router1's RIP configuration.

The agent's investigation log provides concrete command outputs (router configs, RIP status, ping failures, tc stats) that support the claim router1 lacks RIP and that cross-segment traffic fails due to missing routes. The inferences from those observations to the diagnosis and proposed fix follow logically and the key alternatives (no RIP, no learned routes, pings showing unreachable) were tested.
